entries.quote: The craftsman is not an individual expressing individual whims, but a part of the universe, giving expression to ideals of eternal beauty and unchanging laws
entries.description: Epigraph by Ananda Coomaraswamy framing craftsmanship as expression of eternal beauty and unchanging laws, not individual whim.
entries.importance_reason: Epigraph: sets the chapter's philosophy but is not itself examinable chapter content; no architectural fact is stated.
entries.question_suitability_reason: An epigraph attribution question would test the quote, not chapter knowledge; the quote states no checkable architectural fact.
entries.context_needed: None for attribution; the philosophical framing only makes sense as the chapter epigraph.

entries.quote: 1. What role has architecture played in the Indian civilisation? 2. What are some of the key concepts and developments behind Indian architecture? 3. How is the heritage of Indian architecture of relevance today?
entries.description: The chapter's three Big Questions: architecture's role in Indian civilisation; key concepts and developments; relevance of the heritage today.
entries.importance_reason: They define what the chapter is trying to teach, but they are questions, not answers; the answers are the entries that follow.
entries.question_suitability_reason: These are open inquiry questions, not facts with a single correct answer.

entries.quote: 'Architecture' - the art and techniques of design and construction, which combine functional and aesthetic aspects - is not only an art but also a highly technical field, in which India has excelled for several millennia.
entries.description: Definition of architecture (art + techniques of design and construction, functional and aesthetic) and the claim that India has excelled in this highly technical field for several millennia.
entries.importance_reason: The chapter's opening definition; the functional-plus-aesthetic duality recurs in every section (temples, mosques, forts, houses).
entries.question_suitability_reason: Self-contained definition; stem can state the definition and ask what it defines, or vice versa.

entries.quote: these accomplishments have evolved in time and developed great geographical diversity
entries.description: Indian architecture evolved over time and developed great geographical diversity.
entries.importance_reason: The chapter's organising thesis: chronological evolution plus regional diversity, demonstrated by every section that follows.
entries.question_suitability_reason: A stem can state the two dimensions (time, geography) without chapter context.

entries.quote: we will go on a journey, visiting a few representative structures or monuments grouped in a few categories
entries.description: Chapter method: a journey through a few representative structures/monuments grouped in categories, not an exhaustive survey; guided by the map (Fig. 3.3, locations) and the timeline (Fig. 3.2, river of time).
entries.importance_reason: Explains the chapter's selective scope (representative, not exhaustive) and points to the two orientation figures; the closing section repeats the 'leaves out thousands' caveat.
entries.question_suitability_reason: States chapter method, not an architectural fact; a question on it would test the book's organisation, not the subject.

entries.quote: Harappan architecture represents the earliest known tradition of urban planning and construction in the Indian subcontinent.
entries.description: Harappan architecture is the earliest known tradition of urban planning and construction in the Indian subcontinent.
entries.importance_reason: Chronological primacy claim that anchors the whole chapter ('The Beginnings'); 'earliest known' is a classic exam formulation.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Self-contained superlative claim; stem can ask which tradition is the earliest known.

entries.quote: It is characterised by carefully laid-out cities, standardised urban concepts, and an emphasis on drainage, water management, and civic organisation.
entries.description: Harappan architecture's characteristics: carefully laid-out cities, standardised urban concepts, emphasis on drainage, water management and civic organisation.
entries.importance_reason: The defining characteristic list for Harappan urbanism; drainage/water management is then demonstrated by Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira and the water-structures section.
entries.question_suitability_reason: A list-type stem (which features characterise Harappan architecture) is fully self-contained.

entries.description: Most Harappan cities were built with bricks BECAUSE they stood in alluvial plains where clay is abundant (material follows local availability).
entries.importance_reason: Explicit causal relationship (local material determines building material) that the chapter repeats as a pattern (Dholavira stone, Lingaraja sandstone/laterite, Dilwara Aravalli marble, Agra Dholpur sandstone).
entries.question_suitability_reason: Cause-and-effect stem is self-contained ('Why were most Harappan cities built of brick?').

entries.description: Mohenjo-daro, in present-day Sindh, Pakistan, was an extensive city.

entries.quote: From the 4th or 3rd century BCE onward, with the rise of Buddhism several new architectural forms emerged in north India, slowly spreading to other regions.
entries.description: From the 4th or 3rd century BCE onward, the rise of Buddhism brought several new architectural forms in north India, slowly spreading to other regions.
entries.importance_reason: Dates the Buddhist architectural turn and links it causally to Buddhism's rise; frames the whole stupa section.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Date range + cause + spread are self-contained.

entries.importance_reason: The section's core definition plus scale and materials in one sentence.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Definition stem is fully self-contained.

entries.quote: The larger ones became complex ritual centres with railings, gateways, and elaborate panels often narrating episodes in the Buddha's life.
entries.description: Larger stupas became complex ritual centres with railings, gateways and elaborate panels often narrating episodes in the Buddha's life.

entries.question_suitability_reason: Component list is self-contained.
entries.uncertainty: 'Often' preserved for the narrative panels.

entries.description: At this early stage the Buddha was represented symbolically (footprints, wheel of dharma, or the stupa itself) rather than in human form.

entries.quote: DON'T MISS OUT (box set, p. 96) - four entries: Sharada Peetha Temple; Hidimba Devi Temple; Jageshwar Group of Temples; The Golden Temple
entries.description: STRUCTURE record: p. 96 is a full-page DON'T MISS OUT box set with four entries (inventoried individually as INV-3-041 to INV-3-048). The box format itself matters for extraction: the pipeline merges all four entries into a single body block (see matrix), so entry boundaries survive only because the box headings are inline in the text.

entries.question_suitability_reason: Box organisation, not content.

entries.quote: Dedicated to Goddess Sharada (a form of Sarasvati), Sharada Peetha was a renowned centre of learning and a key site in the development of the Sharada script.
entries.description: Sharada Peetha (Jammu and Kashmir): dedicated to Goddess Sharada, a form of Sarasvati; a renowned centre of learning and a key site in the development of the Sharada script.
entries.importance_reason: Dedication + learning-centre + script-development roles make this the box's most distinctive content; the script link is unique in the chapter.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Dedication, function and script link are self-contained.

entries.quote: Attracting scholars from different parts of India and the world, it flourished between the 6th and 12th centuries CE, and its legacy earned Kashmir the name Sharada Desh (the land of Sharada). Though now in ruins, it remains an important part of India's archaeological and cultural heritage.
entries.description: Sharada Peetha attracted scholars from India and the world, flourished between the 6th and 12th centuries CE, and its legacy earned Kashmir the name Sharada Desh (the land of Sharada); now in ruins, it remains important archaeological and cultural heritage.
entries.importance_reason: Flourishing period + the Sharada Desh name are the box's two most quotable facts.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Period + derived place-name are self-contained.

entries.quote: Located in Manali amid the cedar forests of Dhungiri Van Vihar, the Hidimba Devi Temple is one of the oldest religious sites in the Kullu Valley. Built in the 16th century CE, the shrine is dedicated to Hidimba (Hirama), the wife of Bhima from the Mahabharata.
entries.description: Hidimba Devi Temple, Manali, amid the cedar forests of Dhungiri Van Vihar: one of the oldest religious sites in the Kullu Valley, built in the 16th century CE, dedicated to Hidimba (Hirama), wife of Bhima from the Mahabharata.
entries.importance_reason: Place + date + dedication + epic link in one box entry; a complete self-contained item.
entries.question_suitability_reason: All elements are stated in the box text.

entries.quote: A nearby temple dedicated to their son, Ghatotkacha, further reflects the site's close association with the epic tradition.
entries.description: A nearby temple dedicated to Hidimba and Bhima's son Ghatotkacha further reflects the site's close association with the epic tradition.
entries.importance_reason: Secondary corroborating detail for the Mahabharata association; depends on the Hidimba entry for sense.
entries.question_suitability_reason: With Hidimba/Bhima named in the stem, the Ghatotkacha temple detail is answerable.
entries.context_needed: The Hidimba Devi Temple entry (who Hidimba and Bhima are).

entries.quote: The Jageshwar Group of Temples, located in the JataGanga Valley of Uttarakhand's Almora district, is an ancient temple complex associated with the Katyuri, Chand, and Gurjara-Pratihara dynasties (8th-18th centuries).
entries.description: Jageshwar Group of Temples, JataGanga Valley, Almora district, Uttarakhand: ancient complex associated with the Katyuri, Chand and Gurjara-Pratihara dynasties (8th-18th centuries).
entries.importance_reason: Place + dynasty association + ten-century span; the dynasty list is distinctive chapter content.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Place + dynasties + period are self-contained.
entries.uncertainty: The 8th-18th centuries span attaches to the dynasty association in the source sentence; it is not a construction date for the temples as a group.

entries.quote: Comprising about 124 stone temples, it is renowned for its Swayambhu Linga, known as Nagesh Darukavane. The garbha griha houses Jageshwara Mahadeva, who is locally revered as Bala Jageshwara ('Child Shiva').
entries.description: Jageshwar comprises about 124 stone temples; it is renowned for its Swayambhu Linga known as Nagesh Darukavane; the garbha griha houses Jageshwara Mahadeva, locally revered as Bala Jageshwara ('Child Shiva').
entries.importance_reason: Count + named linga + local name of the deity; the 'about 124' count is a classic exam number.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Count and names are self-contained.
entries.uncertainty: Count is approximate ('about 124').

entries.quote: The gurudwara is the place of worship of the Sikhs.
entries.description: A gurudwara is the place of worship of the Sikhs.
entries.importance_reason: Foundational term definition for the Golden Temple entry; a basic exam definition.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Term + definition are self-contained.

entries.quote: The Harmandir Sahib or Golden Temple in Punjab is considered to be the holiest of the Sikh Shrines. The temple was founded by Guru Ramdas Sahib the 4th of the 10th Sikh Gurus. The construction of the temple and its sarovar was continued by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru in 1588.
entries.description: Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple), Punjab: considered the holiest of Sikh shrines; founded by Guru Ramdas Sahib, the 4th of the 10 Sikh Gurus; construction of the temple and its sarovar continued by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1588.
entries.importance_reason: Name + superlative + two-Guru succession + date; complete self-contained item.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Names, order (4th/5th) and date are all stated.
entries.uncertainty: AMBIGUOUS ATTACHMENT: the sentence leaves it slightly unclear whether 'in 1588' dates Arjan Dev's continuation or is a looser date for the phase; record as written, do not rephrase as 'built in 1588'.

entries.quote: For several millennia, India's monsoon-driven climate has led people to develop a great variety of structures for the harvesting, storage and distribution of water.
entries.description: India's monsoon-driven climate led people over several millennia to develop a great variety of structures for harvesting, storage and distribution of water.
entries.importance_reason: The section's causal thesis (climate → water architecture) and its three functions, which organise every example that follows.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Cause + three functions are self-contained.

entries.quote: These structures, whether simple (such as a humble village pond) or highly sophisticated (such as the Grand Anicut, see chapter 'The Age of Reorganisation' in the Grade 7 textbook), have been very diverse owing to the different geological, climatic and environmental conditions of the land, from the Himalayan foothills, the Thar Desert, the Gangetic plains, the Western Ghats, to the Deccan plateau or the Northeast.
entries.description: Water structures range from simple (village pond) to highly sophisticated (Grand Anicut, a Grade 7 cross-reference) and are diverse owing to geological, climatic and environmental conditions across regions: Himalayan foothills, Thar Desert, Gangetic plains, Western Ghats, Deccan plateau, Northeast.
entries.importance_reason: The diversity claim plus a region list; the Grand Anicut itself is not taught in this chapter (cross-reference only).
entries.question_suitability_reason: The region list and simple-vs-sophisticated contrast are self-contained; the Grand Anicut should not be asked as chapter content.
entries.uncertainty: Grand Anicut is a cross-reference, not a chapter-taught example; do not treat it as a taught structure.

entries.quote: This tradition goes all the way back to the Harappan civilisation; remember Dholavira's large reservoirs, for instance.
entries.description: The water-structure tradition goes back to the Harappan civilisation; Dholavira's large reservoirs are the cited example.
entries.importance_reason: Continuity link back to the Harappan section; the Dholavira reservoirs were not detailed earlier (they appear here first as an example, and in the Fig. 3.7 plan caption).
entries.question_suitability_reason: Antiquity + example are self-contained.
entries.visual_dependency: low - Dholavira reservoirs also labelled in the Fig. 3.7 plan

entries.quote: the Harappans invented wells that cannot collapse inward under the pressure of underground infiltration, thanks to their trapezoid-shaped bricks that lock together (Fig. 3.14).
entries.description: Harappans invented wells that cannot collapse inward under underground infiltration pressure, thanks to trapezoid-shaped bricks that lock together (Fig. 3.14: a simplified sketch of a typical Harappan well).
entries.importance_reason: A distinctive Harappan engineering claim (invention + mechanism + brick shape); highly question-ready.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Invention + mechanism + brick shape are self-contained.
entries.visual_dependency: low - Fig. 3.14 sketch illustrates the trapezoid bricks

entries.quote: Shringverpur in Uttar Pradesh was known as Shringaverapura in the Ramayana (which describes it as the place where Rama, Sita and Lakshmana crossed the Ganga while starting on their exile).
entries.description: Shringaverpur (Uttar Pradesh) was known as Shringaverapura in the Ramayana, described there as the place where Rama, Sita and Lakshmana crossed the Ganga at the start of their exile.
entries.importance_reason: Literary-historical identity of the site; the excavation facts that follow carry more architectural weight.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Old name + epic episode + place are self-contained.
entries.uncertainty: Source spells the modern name 'Shringverpur' in this sentence and 'Shringaverpur' in the timeline and Fig. 3.15 caption; both spellings are the same site.

entries.quote: Excavations there brought to light a series of large interconnected reservoirs (Fig. 3.15) fed by a channel from the Ganga during the river's seasonal flooding. The first reservoir or two allowed the silt suspended in water to settle down - a fairly common design.
entries.description: Excavations at Shringaverpur revealed large interconnected reservoirs fed by a Ganga channel during seasonal flooding; the first reservoir or two allowed suspended silt to settle, a fairly common design.
entries.importance_reason: The section's most detailed hydraulic example: source, feeding mechanism and the silt-settling function of the first reservoirs.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Feeding + settling function are self-contained.
entries.visual_dependency: low - Fig. 3.15 shows one of the tanks

entries.quote: Yet the precise working of the entire complex remains to be figured out.
entries.description: The precise working of the entire Shringaverpur reservoir complex remains to be figured out (explicitly unknown).
entries.importance_reason: Models honest limits of knowledge; prevents over-claiming about the complex, but is a negative statement rather than positive content.
entries.question_suitability_reason: A stem can ask what remains unknown about Shringaverpur; the answer ('its precise working') is stated. The stem must not ask HOW it worked.
entries.uncertainty: This is a stated unknown, not a gap in this inventory.

entries.quote: Wells have been constructed in many sizes and shapes from bricks, stones, or terracotta ring.
entries.description: Wells have been constructed in many sizes and shapes from bricks, stones or terracotta ring.
entries.importance_reason: General well-construction statement bridging Harappan wells to the stepwell tradition.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Materials list is self-contained.
entries.uncertainty: 'Terracotta ring' is the source's phrasing (singular 'ring' for ring segments).

entries.quote: In classical times, a tradition of stepwells (vavs or baoris) developed in Gujarat and Rajasthan, many of them engineering marvels as well as spectacular works of art.
entries.description: In classical times a stepwell tradition (vavs or baoris) developed in Gujarat and Rajasthan; many stepwells were engineering marvels as well as spectacular works of art.
entries.importance_reason: Defines stepwells (with both regional names), their place, period and dual character (engineering + art).
entries.question_suitability_reason: Term + names + place + period are self-contained.

entries.quote: The stepwell at Rani ki Vav (Fig. 3.16) has multiple pillared levels and hundreds of magnificent statues.
entries.description: Rani ki Vav stepwell has multiple pillared levels and hundreds of magnificent statues.
entries.importance_reason: The named exemplar's distinguishing features; the 'hundreds of statues' scale is distinctive.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Features are self-contained.
entries.uncertainty: No date for Rani ki Vav is given in body text; the timeline's '1010 CE' label is unpaired (see INV-3-007) and must not be attached without visual confirmation.

entries.quote: Besides harvesting and storing rainwater, stepwells offered a social space where people could sit together, enjoy cooler temperatures and exchange all the news.
entries.description: Besides harvesting and storing rainwater, stepwells offered a social space where people could sit together, enjoy cooler temperatures and exchange news.
entries.importance_reason: The social function of stepwells beyond water storage; a classic 'besides X, also Y' exam formulation.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Water function + social function are self-contained.

entries.quote: Temples often had water reservoirs or pushkarinis attached to them, which were used for water harvesting as well as water-based rituals. Many of them were also works of art, with numerous stairways built into them (Fig. 3.17).
entries.description: Temples often had attached water reservoirs (pushkarinis) used for water harvesting and water-based rituals; many were works of art with numerous stairways built into them (Fig. 3.17: a pushkarini at Vijayanagara).
entries.importance_reason: Links temple architecture to water architecture and defines pushkarini by function; the Vijayanagara example grounds it.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Term + two functions + stairway feature are self-contained.
entries.visual_dependency: low - Fig. 3.17 photograph of the Vijayanagara pushkarini

entries.quote: Many of these traditional water structures suffer today from depleted water sources, maintenance issues, pollution, waste dumping, etc. Environmentalists, locals, and NGOs sometimes join hands to preserve them, but much remains to be done.
entries.description: Today many traditional water structures suffer from depleted water sources, maintenance issues, pollution and waste dumping; environmentalists, locals and NGOs sometimes join hands to preserve them, but much remains to be done.
entries.importance_reason: The section's present-day threats-and-preservation point, echoed in the closing section (p. 123); 'sometimes' and 'much remains' are the honest qualifiers.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Threat list + preservation actors are self-contained.

entries.quote: With antecedents in the stupa and rock-cut types of architecture, temples have been central to India's cultural life for many centuries. Whether Buddhist, Jain or Hindu, temples have been places of worship, but also of learning, literature, art (sculpture, dance, music, painting among others). Besides, they were centres of social intercourse and economic life.
entries.description: Temples (Buddhist, Jain or Hindu), with antecedents in stupa and rock-cut architecture, have been central to India's cultural life for centuries: places of worship and also of learning, literature and art (sculpture, dance, music, painting), and centres of social intercourse and economic life.
entries.importance_reason: The temple section's thesis: multi-functionality across three religions, with antecedents explicitly linking back to the two previous sections.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Religions + functions list are self-contained.

entries.quote: Architecturally, they evolved into works of art that celebrate life and encourage bhakti as well as quiet contemplation.
entries.description: Architecturally temples evolved into works of art celebrating life and encouraging bhakti as well as quiet contemplation.
entries.importance_reason: Aesthetic-spiritual characterisation; supports the symbolism entries that follow but is more general than they are.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Celebration + bhakti + contemplation are self-contained as a characterisation.

entries.quote: Classical temples emerged during the Gupta era. Many were built thanks to royal patronage, as evidenced by inscriptions, but also by endowments from various donors.
entries.description: Classical temples emerged during the Gupta era; many were built through royal patronage (evidenced by inscriptions) and also through endowments from various donors.
entries.importance_reason: Emergence period + two funding sources (patronage, endowments) with the inscription evidence note.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Period + funding sources are self-contained.

entries.quote: Temple construction followed principles and techniques spelt out in treatises of shilpashastra - the discipline of arts and crafts, largely dedicated to architecture and sculpture.
entries.description: Temple construction followed principles and techniques in shilpashastra treatises; shilpashastra is the discipline of arts and crafts, largely dedicated to architecture and sculpture.
entries.importance_reason: Names the theoretical discipline governing temple construction; a standard definition question.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Term + definition + scope are self-contained.

entries.quote: A temple's main elements are shown in Fig. 3.18: a ceremonial entrance (gopuram in south India; torana in some north Indian temples), one or several mandapas (pillared halls), and the garbhagriha, the innermost chamber where the image (murti) of the deity is kept.
entries.description: A temple's main elements: ceremonial entrance (gopuram in south India; torana in some north Indian temples), one or several mandapas (pillared halls), and the garbhagriha, the innermost chamber where the deity's image (murti) is kept.
entries.importance_reason: The section's component list with north/south entrance terminology; every element term recurs in later temple entries.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Component list + regional terms are self-contained without the plan.
entries.context_needed: None (the plan reference can be dropped).
entries.visual_dependency: low - Fig. 3.18 plan; its labels (secondary shrines, prakara, pradakshina corridor, 'from outer to inner') are visual-only (see INV-3-069)

entries.quote: Above the garbhagriha is a tower called shikhara (in north Indian temples) or vimana (in south Indian temples). The main alignment is generally east-west, with the garbhagriha facing east.
entries.description: Above the garbhagriha stands a tower called shikhara in north Indian temples or vimana in south Indian temples; the main alignment is generally east-west, with the garbhagriha facing east.
entries.importance_reason: The north/south tower naming contrast plus the east-west orientation rule; both are standard exam points.
entries.question_suitability_reason: North/south terms + orientation are self-contained.
entries.uncertainty: Alignment is 'generally' east-west; keep the qualifier.

entries.quote: Fig. 3.18. Simplified ground plan of the Brihadishvara Temple
entries.description: Fig. 3.18 is a simplified ground plan of the Brihadishvara Temple, whose labels include: garbhagriha, mandapa, secondary shrines, prakara, pradakshina corridor, gopuram, and the direction note 'from outer to inner'.
entries.importance_reason: The plan's spatial vocabulary (prakara = enclosure, pradakshina corridor) is taught visually here; the body text defines prakara later (p. 101) but the corridor layout is plan-only.
entries.question_suitability_reason: The spatial arrangement (what lies where, 'from outer to inner') can only be assessed against the plan itself.
entries.uncertainty: Plan labels are text in the PDF but their spatial relationships are visual; the 'prakara' enclosure concept is confirmed in body text on p. 101.

entries.quote: both horizontally and vertically, a temple is planned as a representation of the human body - that of Purusha or the cosmic being.
entries.description: A temple is planned, both horizontally and vertically, as a representation of the human body: that of Purusha, the cosmic being.
entries.importance_reason: The section's central philosophical claim, developed vertically in the next entry and posed as a horizontal exercise for students.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Body-as-temple correspondence is self-contained.
entries.visual_dependency: low - Fig. 3.19 illustrates the vertical equivalence

entries.quote: Fig. 3.19 shows the vertical equivalence: from the top of the shikhara or vimana, which corresponds to the head, down to the platform on which the temple rests, which corresponds to the feet (you need not remember the technical terms for the shikhara's different parts shown in Fig. 3.19).
entries.description: Vertical equivalence (Fig. 3.19): the top of the shikhara/vimana corresponds to the head, down to the platform the temple rests on, which corresponds to the feet. The source explicitly says students need not remember the technical terms for the shikhara's different parts shown in Fig. 3.19.
entries.importance_reason: The head-to-feet mapping is the testable content; the 'need not remember' instruction is a binding scope limit for any question on Fig. 3.19.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Head/feet mapping is self-contained; the part-names must NOT be asked, per the source's own instruction.
entries.uncertainty: The intermediate part-names in Fig. 3.19 are visual-only and explicitly excluded from required learning; they are not transcribed here.

entries.quote: Temple worship can be understood as a journey from the outer world (left behind once one crosses the entrance) to the inner world awaiting the worshipper in the garbhagriha, mirroring our own spiritual journey.
entries.description: Temple worship as a journey from the outer world (left behind at the entrance) to the inner world in the garbhagriha, mirroring the worshipper's own spiritual journey.
entries.importance_reason: Interpretive framing of the temple experience; supports the outer-to-inner plan logic but is reflective rather than factual.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Outer-to-inner journey metaphor is self-contained as an interpretation question ('How can temple worship be understood?').

entries.quote: Until the 8th or 9th century, temples were modest in size. From the 10th century onward, in different parts of India they grew in scale and began incorporating multiple shrines, amenities, and enclosures (prakaras), culminating in vast complexes.
entries.description: Until the 8th or 9th century temples were modest in size; from the 10th century onward they grew in scale, incorporating multiple shrines, amenities and enclosures (prakaras), culminating in vast complexes.
entries.importance_reason: The scale trajectory of classical temples, with the prakara (enclosure) term defined in use; frames Brihadisvara and Lingaraja as culmination examples.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Two-period contrast + features are self-contained.

entries.quote: we saw the magnificent Kandariya Mahadeva Temple of Khajuraho and Cambodia's colossal Angkor Wat Temple
entries.description: Cross-referenced large-temple examples from the Grade 7 textbook: Kandariya Mahadeva Temple of Khajuraho and Cambodia's colossal Angkor Wat Temple.
entries.importance_reason: Cross-references illustrating the 'vast complexes' point; neither temple is taught in this chapter.
entries.question_suitability_reason: These are pointers to another textbook's content; asking about them would test Grade 7 material, not this chapter.
entries.context_needed: Grade 7 textbook chapter 'Turning Tides: 11th and 12th Centuries'.

entries.quote: In Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, the imposing Brihadishvara Temple (Fig. 3.20) was built by Rajaraja Chola I around 1010. It is renowned for its vast mandapas, a huge vimana, over 60 metres high, and a massive Nandi (sacred bull) statue carved from a single stone, which sits in a pavilion facing the main shrine.
entries.description: Brihadishvara Temple, Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu: built by Rajaraja Chola I around 1010; renowned for vast mandapas, a huge vimana over 60 metres high, and a massive Nandi (sacred bull) statue carved from a single stone in a pavilion facing the main shrine.
entries.importance_reason: The section's flagship temple with builder, date, vimana height and single-stone Nandi; the most question-dense entry in the temple section.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Builder + date + height + Nandi are self-contained.
entries.uncertainty: DATE DISCREPANCY: body text says 'around 1010'; the Fig. 3.2 timeline carries a '1063 CE' label that appears near the Brihadisvara entry (pairing unverified, see INV-3-007). Use 'around 1010' from body text; do not use 1063 CE until the timeline is read visually.
entries.visual_dependency: low - Fig. 3.20 photograph; Fig. 3.21 panel detail follows on p. 102

entries.quote: The entire structure showcases exquisite craftsmanship, with intricate granite carvings and sculptures adorning its walls (Fig. 3.21).
entries.description: Brihadishvara's entire structure shows exquisite craftsmanship, with intricate granite carvings and sculptures adorning its walls (Fig. 3.21: a panel depicting Mahalakshmi, attendants and minor deities).
entries.importance_reason: Material (granite) + decoration detail completing the Brihadishvara description; the Fig. 3.21 panel subject is caption detail.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Granite carvings claim is self-contained; the Mahalakshmi panel subject needs the caption and is secondary.

entries.quote: Both the Brihadishvara Temple and the Lingaraja Temple in Bhubaneswar, Odisha (Fig. 3.22), are dedicated to Shiva, with several secondary shrines dedicated to goddess Parvati and other deities.
entries.description: Both Brihadishvara and Lingaraja (Bhubaneswar, Odisha) are dedicated to Shiva, with several secondary shrines dedicated to goddess Parvati and other deities.
entries.importance_reason: Shared dedication + secondary-shrine pattern linking the two flagship temples; a natural comparison question.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Shared dedication is self-contained.

entries.quote: Built in the early 11th century, the Lingaraja Temple has three large mandapas used for different purposes. It is built from locally available sandstone and laterite stone and is rich in ornate carvings (Fig. 3.23).
entries.description: Lingaraja Temple, Bhubaneswar: built in the early 11th century; three large mandapas used for different purposes; built from locally available sandstone and laterite stone; rich in ornate carvings (Fig. 3.23: a detail of its shikhara).
entries.importance_reason: The second flagship temple with date, mandapa count, local materials (again the local-material pattern) and carving richness.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Date + mandapas + materials are self-contained.

entries.quote: The Dilwara Temples at Mount Abu, Rajasthan, are a group of five exquisitely carved Jain temples built between the 11th and 13th centuries by the Solanki or Chaulukya dynasty. Made of white marble procured from the nearby Aravalli hills, they feature delicate carvings of the Jain tirthankaras, deities, dancers, musicians, and ornamental patterns that cover every surface.
entries.description: Dilwara Temples, Mount Abu, Rajasthan: group of five exquisitely carved Jain temples built between the 11th and 13th centuries by the Solanki (Chaulukya) dynasty; white marble from the nearby Aravalli hills; delicate carvings of Jain tirthankaras, deities, dancers, musicians and ornamental patterns covering every surface.
entries.importance_reason: Complete Jain-temple exemplar with count, dates, dynasty, material source and carving subjects; contrasts with the Shiva temples and with Bishnupur brick.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Count + dates + dynasty + material + carvings are self-contained.
entries.visual_dependency: low - Figs. 3.24/3.25 (temple view; pillared hall interior)

entries.quote: Built in the 17th and 18th centuries, the terracotta temples of Bishnupur in West Bengal are of a very different style. They are brick structures with elaborate surface decorations on square panels, many of which depict themes associated with Radha, Krishna or Rama, as well as, scenes from everyday life.
entries.description: Bishnupur terracotta temples, West Bengal, 17th-18th centuries: a very different style; brick structures with elaborate surface decorations on square panels depicting Radha, Krishna or Rama themes and scenes from everyday life.
entries.importance_reason: The deliberate stylistic contrast to Dilwara (marble Jain vs brick terracotta); material + panel subjects are distinctive.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Place + dates + material + panel subjects are self-contained.
entries.uncertainty: DATE TENSION: body text says 17th-18th centuries; the Fig. 3.2 timeline carries a '17th-19th centuries' label near the Bishnupur/Havelis area (pairing unverified, see INV-3-007). Use body-text dates.

entries.quote: Terracotta panels such as those seen in Fig. 3.27 were first carved by hand and then fired in a kiln in a precise manner.
entries.description: Terracotta panels were first carved by hand and then fired in a kiln in a precise manner.
entries.importance_reason: The making process behind Bishnupur's decoration; a two-step technique fact.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Two-step process is self-contained.

entries.quote: note the pyramidal shape of Brihadishvara Temple's vimana
entries.description: Observation from a LET'S EXPLORE prompt: Brihadishvara Temple's vimana has a pyramidal shape (to be compared with the shapes in Fig. 3.19 and with Angkor Wat and Kandariya Mahadeva).
entries.importance_reason: The vimana's pyramidal shape is stated only inside this activity prompt; it is the chapter's one shape description of the Brihadishvara vimana.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Shape attribution is self-contained once stated; the comparison activity itself is not a question.
entries.context_needed: None for the shape claim; the Fig. 3.19 comparison needs the figure.
entries.uncertainty: Stated inside a student activity, not in body prose; flagged as such.
entries.visual_dependency: medium - comparison requires Figs. 3.19/3.24 and the Grade 7 pictures

entries.quote: Did you notice that none of the structures discussed so far use any cement mortar?
entries.description: Factual claim embedded in a LET'S EXPLORE prompt: none of the structures discussed so far (up to p. 104) use any cement mortar.
entries.importance_reason: A striking negative generalisation across all structures covered to that point; useful precisely because it is chapter-scope-dependent.
entries.question_suitability_reason: Usable only if the stem states the scope ('the structures discussed in this chapter up to the classical temples'); as a bare 'Indian structures use no cement mortar' it would be false in general.
entries.context_needed: Chapter scope up to p. 104 (structures discussed so far).
entries.uncertainty: Scope is 'so far' in the chapter; do not generalise to all Indian architecture.

entries.quote: Apart from a large manpower and accomplished sculptors, the architecture of classical temples required highly skilled architects, engineers and craftsmen, as it involved elaborate construction techniques. Recent studies have shown that their planning involved a good deal of mathematics, especially some advanced geometry.

entries.quote: Anyone travelling through India and visiting some of the lesser-known monuments will notice that many are in a state of neglect. Preserving this heritage is indeed very challenging: how to adequately conserve India's thousands of monuments, many of them centuries-old? Government bodies are theoretically responsible for this huge task, but in practice, much will be lost unless citizens feel equally responsible and, to begin with, learn to appreciate and admire this labour of our ancestors. If you revisit our Constitution's 'Fundamental Duties', you will now understand the wisdom of one of them: '... to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture'.
